channel.title: TaskIAP journal
channel.description: Sticky notes, journal entries and reports on construction project management.

item.title: Every Date Needs a Because
item.description: "The pour is Thursday." Why Thursday? Somebody knows: the rebar inspection is booked Wednesday afternoon, and the pump truck is free Thursday. The schedule just shows a bar starting Thursday.

item.title: Panama: Build the Railroad Before You Dig
item.description: France started the Panama Canal in 1881 and gave up after years of work, with thousands of workers dead from yellow fever and malaria and a sea-level design the ground wouldn't allow.

item.title: How the Panama Canal Got Built
item.description: France spent eight years and thousands of lives and failed. The United States finished it in ten. The difference was mostly planning: health, housing, logistics and a design that fit the ground.

item.title: Why does a quiet site worry me?
item.description: If nobody jokes, nobody is passing on what they know either. The stick figures on the trailer whiteboard might be the best safety system we have.

item.title: Measure Time to Tools
item.description: The shift starts at 7:00. The first tool touches the work at 7:50. In between: the toolbox talk, a permit that isn't signed yet, a hunt for the right fittings, a wait for the hoist.

item.title: Stop Typing Percent Complete
item.description: On most status reports, percent complete is a number somebody types. It creeps up a few points a week, because nobody wants the argument, then parks at 95 for three months.

item.title: What do you do with the person who annoys everyone?
item.description: Find the job where their habit pays. The one who checks every bolt callout should be checking bolt callouts.

item.title: Spring Load Restrictions Close the Roads
item.description: Every spring, as the frost comes out of the ground, many Ontario roads go on reduced load limits. A precast delivery or a crane that moved easily in February may not be allowed down the same road in April.

item.title: The Lessons File Nobody Opens
item.description: Every job ends with a lessons-learned report. It goes into the closeout binder, and the next team never opens it. They're busy, it's forty pages, and half the lessons are "communicate better".

item.title: Why do some crews act like they're just passing through?
item.description: Maybe because we treat them that way. Nobody who does their paperwork on a truck tailgate thinks they belong.

item.title: Lags Hide Reasons
item.description: A five-day lag between two activities is usually one of three things: concrete curing, a permit or inspection, or a guess somebody made two years ago. The schedule can't tell you which.

item.title: The Empire State Building Was a Logistics Job
item.description: The Empire State Building went up in about thirteen months in 1930 and 1931, with the steel frame rising several floors a week. It finished early and under budget.

item.title: A Change Costs More in the Field Than on Paper
item.description: A change order prices the added work: material, hours, markup. It rarely prices what the change does to everything around it. Crews get pulled off sequence, finished work gets torn out, and the same room gets visited three times.

item.title: Why is field data still on paper?
item.description: Not the phones and not the policy. The apps need gloves, rain and ten seconds, and most of them were designed at a desk.

item.title: Ask "Waiting on What?" Until You Hit a Name
item.description: Ask why a task isn't done and it takes three phone calls to find out. The crew is waiting on scaffold. Scaffold is waiting on a permit. The permit is waiting on a signature from someone at a cottage with no signal.

item.title: Winter Heat Is a Line Item
item.description: Concrete poured in an Ontario January needs hoarding, heaters, fuel, blankets and someone checking temperatures overnight. None of it shows up as an activity, so it never gets planned. It gets found, one cold morning at a time.

item.title: Hold the Lessons Session Before Everyone Leaves
item.description: The usual lessons-learned meeting happens at closeout, when the superintendent who lived through the foundations has been on another job for a year and the foreman who solved the tie-in has retired.

item.title: Why do hand-drawn roadmaps last so long?
item.description: Nobody can prove them wrong. No dates, no logic, no owners. That is a feature, if you are the one who drew it.

item.title: The Quebec Bridge: Two Collapses and What They Taught
item.description: The longest cantilever span in the world fell twice while it was being built, killing 88 workers. The first collapse is still taught as a case of a warning that couldn't travel fast enough.

item.title: Show What Changed in the Plan
item.description: Each monthly update arrives as a new set of PDFs. To find out what changed, someone lays last month's beside this month's and squints. Most people don't, so changes slip through: a finish moved a week, a tie got deleted, a duration got shorter for no reason.

item.title: Is a 30-second video the best claims insurance there is?
item.description: Probably. Most disputes are about what the area looked like on a Tuesday, and someone had a phone in their pocket that Tuesday.

item.title: Sydney Opera House: Building Before the Design Was Done
item.description: The Sydney Opera House was meant to take four years. It took fourteen, opening in 1973, at many times the original estimate.

item.title: Overtime Borrows From Next Month
item.description: One Saturday recovers a day. Six weeks of Saturdays doesn't recover six days. People get tired, make more mistakes, get hurt more, and start missing Mondays. Hours go up and output per hour goes down.

item.title: Price Risks in Days, Not Colours
item.description: A heat map puts a risk in a red square. The square doesn't say what the risk does to the finish date, so the meeting argues about whether it's red or orange.

item.title: Who signs when the signer is on vacation?
item.description: Usually nobody, until somebody panics. Write the delegation down with an end date, before the vacation.

item.title: Locates Expire Too
item.description: In Ontario you call for locates before you dig, and the marks and paperwork are only good for a limited time. Excavation that slips past the expiry needs new locates, which takes days the schedule didn't plan for.

item.title: Ask What You'd Do Differently on Monday
item.description: "Improve communication with the design team." "Plan procurement earlier." These show up in every lessons report and change nothing, because nobody can act on them.

item.title: Keep Two Weeks of Ready Work
item.description: Work is ready when everything it needs is true at once: drawings issued, material on site, permit signed, area handed over, the work before it finished. One missing piece and it isn't ready, however green it looks on the schedule.

item.title: Why does the consultant's report sound familiar?
item.description: Because the first month was spent interviewing your superintendent. Sometimes you are paying to hear your own people, louder.

item.title: Hoover Dam Couldn't Wait for the Concrete to Cool
item.description: Concrete gives off heat as it cures. Poured as one solid mass, the Hoover Dam would have taken over a century to cool, and cracked as it did.

item.title: Read the Laydown Yard
item.description: Walk the yard before you read the reports. Material that showed up months early is cash already spent, sitting in the rain, getting lost or damaged. Empty racks for next week's work mean a crew is about to stand around.

item.title: How many milestones does a job have?
item.description: On paper, two hundred. In real life, three or four that it lives or dies on. Nobody agrees which ones until one is missed.

item.title: The Crane Is a Predecessor
item.description: Two lifts that need the same crane can't happen at the same time. That's as hard a rule as rebar before concrete. Most schedules keep logic in one place and resources in another, and nobody reconciles them.

item.title: Lessons Learned That Change the Next Job
item.description: Most lessons-learned work produces a report that nobody reads. A few habits turn it into changes the next job can't avoid using.

item.title: Holdback Is a Schedule Item
item.description: Under Ontario's Construction Act, the 10 percent holdback isn't released when the work feels done. It follows a sequence: substantial performance certified and published, then the lien period runs out, then payment.

item.title: Do Band-Aids predict anything?
item.description: Not fatalities. But the same cut from the same knife on the same task, every week, is telling you something cheap to fix.

item.title: Build a Mockup of the Hard Detail
item.description: A curtain wall corner, a firestopped penetration, a shower pan: details that repeat hundreds of times across a building and are easy to get slightly wrong.

item.title: Clear Holds in Batches
item.description: Five hold points need the same inspector this week. They get booked as five separate visits, because five foremen each called on their own.

item.title: Brooklyn Bridge: Bad Wire, Enough Margin
item.description: Partway through spinning the cables of the Brooklyn Bridge, the engineers found that a supplier had been delivering wire that had failed inspection, switched back into the deliveries after it was rejected. Much of it was already in the cables.

item.title: What is the one form everybody fills in?
item.description: The timesheet, because it gets them paid. So put the status question on the timesheet.

item.title: Count Drawing Revisions
item.description: "Design is 90 percent complete" can stay true for a year. A better signal is how many drawings got revised this month, and how many of those were already issued for construction.

item.title: The Schedule Doesn't Know the Site Rules
item.description: No hot work within 10 metres of fuel. Two people for a confined space entry. Hold for the inspector before backfill. Those rules live in a binder, a toolbox talk and the superintendent's head. The schedule knows none of them.

item.title: The Night Shift Needs Its Own Boss
item.description: A second shift gets added to recover time. The superintendent goes home at six, and the night crew works from a list, with nobody on site who can make a decision.

item.title: Is the bad attitude the person or the job?
item.description: Mostly the job, I think. Give someone a ready work front and straight answers and most of the attitude goes away. Not all of it.

item.title: The Utility Connection Is Always Late
item.description: Permanent hydro, gas, water and telecom show up late on job after job. The utility has its own queue, its own design review and its own crews, and none of them are on your schedule.

item.title: Everything on Site Expires
item.description: Permits, scaffold tags, crane certifications, welder qualifications, medicals, insurance certificates, the concrete supplier's mix approval. Almost every condition for work has an end date, and the plan knows none of them.

item.title: Why do so many schedule activities finish on a Friday?
item.description: Half-baked theory: people plan in weeks, not days. The work doesn't care what day it is, so Monday absorbs the slip.

item.title: Quebec Bridge: The Warning Arrived Too Late
item.description: In 1907 the Quebec Bridge collapsed during construction and killed 75 workers. Days before, the inspector on site had reported that steel members were bending.

item.title: Planning From Conditions: The Long Version
item.description: Most schedules are built from activities and logic ties. Most work on site is stopped by something else: a permit, a crane, a missing part, the weather. Here is what changes when you plan from the conditions instead.

item.title: The First Floor Is the Slowest
item.description: Repetitive work speeds up. The tenth floor, the fortieth pipe support and the hundredth panel all go faster than the first, as the crew learns the details, the sequence and each other.

item.title: Has anything ever been 50 percent complete?
item.description: Reports show 10, 90 and 95 all the time. 50 seems to get skipped. I suspect it is the point where people start being careful.

item.title: The Last 5 Percent Takes a Third of the Job
item.description: Deficiency lists, commissioning, turnover documents and closeout routinely eat a third of the calendar. They're planned as the last 5 percent, and nobody manages them until the crews are leaving.

item.title: Count the Crane Picks
item.description: The crane is often the busiest resource on site, and nobody knows how busy. The plan assumes picks per hour; the operator knows what happened.

item.title: Test the Envelope Before the Finishes Go In
item.description: Water finds the one gap in the window flashing, but usually after the drywall is up, the flooring is down and the owner has been invited for a walkthrough.

item.title: How long should a coordination meeting be?
item.description: As long as it takes to get every red item to a name and a date. If that takes two hours, the problem is not the meeting.

item.title: Ask What-If Before the Meeting Ends
item.description: "What happens if the crane is two weeks late?" On most jobs the answer is "let us look at it and get back to you", and the answer comes the following week, after the decision was already made by default.

item.title: Paid by the Mile
item.description: The two companies building the first transcontinental railroad in the 1860s were paid in government bonds and land for each mile of track they laid. So both raced, and quality came second.

item.title: What do the best superintendents have in common?
item.description: They walk the site before they open the laptop. Small sample. Could be a coincidence.

item.title: More People Can Make It Slower
item.description: When a job falls behind, the reflex is to add crews. Put four trades in one room and they wait on each other, block each other's access and damage each other's work. Output per person drops, sometimes far enough that the room finishes later.

item.title: Your Old Schedules Are Your Best Estimating Data
item.description: At closeout, the as-built dates for every activity go into the archive and nobody opens them again. They're the best estimating data a contractor has: its own crews, its own jobs, its own weather.

item.title: Write the Assumption Next to the Estimate
item.description: Every estimate is built on assumptions: the soil is what the geotech report says, the steel arrives in one shipment, the owner picks finishes by spring. They get decided in a hurry and never written down.

item.title: Is a high RFI count bad?
item.description: Not sure. Lots of RFIs can mean bad drawings, or a crew that asks before guessing. The answer time matters more than the count.

item.title: A Near Miss Is a Free Lesson
item.description: A near miss has everything an incident has, except the injury: the same broken process, the same missing barrier, the same rushed decision. It's the same lesson without the cost.

item.title: Why Closeout Takes a Third of the Job
item.description: Deficiency lists, commissioning and turnover get planned as the last 5 percent of the work and managed when the crews are leaving. Here is why that goes wrong and how to run it from the start.

item.title: Merge the Contractors' Plans Before the Site Does
item.description: The civil contractor plans to have the north road closed for trenching next week. The steel contractor plans deliveries down the north road next week. Both schedules are fine on their own.

item.title: Has a lessons-learned report ever changed the next job?
item.description: Only when the lesson got written into a checklist the next team had to use. A report nobody opens teaches nobody.

item.title: Crossrail: The Tunnels Were the Easy Part
item.description: London's Crossrail, now the Elizabeth line, finished its tunnels on time. The line was due to open in December 2018. Months before, it announced a delay, and it opened in May 2022, billions over budget.

item.title: Look Further Ahead Than Your Longest Lead Time
item.description: A three-week lookahead can't catch a constraint that takes four weeks to clear. Permits, engineered supports, crane bookings, outage windows: if clearing one takes longer than the window, it's already late by the time anyone sees it.

item.title: Who owns the float?
item.description: The contract says one thing and everyone acts like it's theirs. My guess: whoever spends it first.

item.title: What It Costs to Ask a Question
item.description: Every site has a price for asking a question. Some of it is time: finding who knows, then waiting for them. Some of it is looking like you should already know. When the price is high, people guess, and some of the guesses get poured in concrete.

item.title: Small Jobs Teach Faster
item.description: A three-year project gives a project manager one chance to learn from the whole cycle. A three-month job gives four a year.

item.title: Photograph Everything Before It's Covered
item.description: Rebar before the pour. Conduit and pipe before the drywall. Underground services before backfill. Once it's covered, it's a guess, and the guess usually costs a saw and a patch.

item.title: What counts as a weather day?
item.description: Whatever the contract says, which is never what the crew thinks. Agree the definition before the first storm, not during it.

item.title: Some Plans Should Be Impossible to Publish
item.description: A schedule can put two crews in one confined space, skip a hold point, or plan a lift over an energized line, and the software will print it in colour.

item.title: The Big Dig and One Wrong Glue
item.description: Boston's Big Dig buried an elevated highway in tunnels. It finished in 2007, years late and billions over the early estimates.

item.title: Count the Handoffs
item.description: Schedules count tasks. Most of what goes wrong happens between them, when work, information or authority passes from one crew, company or system to the next.

item.title: Why does the crane run the job?
item.description: Because it's the one resource every trade needs and nobody can share at the same time. If you want to know the real schedule, read the crane booking sheet.

item.title: Owners Remember the First Week After Handover
item.description: The job can finish on time and under budget, and the owner will still remember that the heat didn't work in the first week, the keys were wrong and nobody answered the phone.

item.title: Put the Owner's Decisions on the Schedule
item.description: Owner decisions hold up work as surely as missing steel: finishes selections, a change approval, a tie-in date, a design question. They rarely appear on the schedule, so they never look late.

item.title: A Short History of Scheduling, From Gantt to Monte Carlo
item.description: Every tool on a scheduler's screen was invented to fix one particular problem. Knowing which problem tells you where each tool is still weak.

item.title: Does anyone remember last week's toolbox talk?
item.description: Probably not the words. Maybe the story, if there was one. So tell a story about something that happened here.

item.title: The Channel Tunnel Met in the Middle
item.description: In 1990 the British and French tunnelling crews broke through to each other under the Channel, having started from opposite coasts many kilometres apart. The two bores met within a fraction of a metre.

item.title: How Long Bad News Takes to Reach the Plan
item.description: Every problem has two dates: the day someone on site first saw it, and the day it showed up in the plan. On most jobs the gap is days or weeks, and the whole time, decisions get made off a plan that's wrong.

item.title: Why does nobody believe the baseline?
item.description: Because everyone knows it was built to win the job, not to run it. Keep it for the contract, and plan from the forecast.

item.title: Not Everything Is a Nuclear Valve
item.description: A temporary laydown pad does not need the paperwork of a pressure boundary. Four days spent perfecting it are four days taken from work that drives the finish.

item.title: ASAP Is Not a Tolerance
item.description: Drawings say ±5 mm. Instructions say "ASAP". The crew can't tell a hold point from a favour, so everything gets treated as urgent, and people burn out on work that could have waited.

item.title: Tell the Crew When to Stop Digging
item.description: "Hydrovac the copper lines, 3 days" gets you three days of digging whether you need it or not. "Hydrovac until you can see the layout, a day at most" tells the crew when they're finished.

item.title: Why does the schedule review take two hours?
item.description: Because we review the whole schedule. The crew only needs the next three weeks and the five things blocking them.

item.title: Float Is Only as Good as the Logic
item.description: One missing tie and an activity shows eight days of slack it doesn't have. One padded duration and a path looks critical when it isn't.

item.title: Don't Pad Dates on Your Suppliers
item.description: Suppliers can tell when your drop-dead date has two weeks of padding in it. Pad it and they stop telling you about trouble in their shop until it's too late to work around.

item.title: The Two-Hour Wall
item.description: The fire code calls for a two-hour wall. That requirement gets copied into the design basis, a wall type, a firestop detail, a QC record and a commissioning check. Then the job closes out and the copies scatter.

item.title: Is a mockup ever a waste of money?
item.description: I haven't seen one that was. The detail that fails in the mockup is the one that would have failed four hundred times on the building.

item.title: A 200-Day Bar Can't Be Late
item.description: Weekly scaffold inspections go in the schedule as one 200-day bar. The bar can't be late, so nobody notices when this week's inspection is.

item.title: Can You Undo It?
item.description: Safety learned to aim at what can kill people, not at what happens most often. Project risk can steal that.

item.title: The Rideau Canal: Building Through the Swamp
item.description: In six years, with hand tools, a British army engineer and a few thousand labourers built a navigable route from Ottawa to Kingston. It cost several times its estimate, it cost hundreds of lives, and it is still in use.

item.title: Why does every Ontario job lose a week in March?
item.description: Mud, frost coming out, load restrictions on the roads, and everyone tired of winter. Plan the week. It shows up anyway.

item.title: Six Welders Aren't a Crew
item.description: The plan prices six welders at a rate. A crew that's worked together all season will beat six welders who met on Monday, at the same rate.

item.title: Weather Comes With a Free Forecast
item.description: Weather is the only project risk that comes with a free, public, daily forecast with probabilities attached. Most schedules still plan a February pour like a June one.

item.title: What is the cheapest schedule fix there is?
item.description: Calling the inspector the day before. Second place: having the material on site before the crew.

item.title: Count the Surprises, and Count the Looking
item.description: You can't list your unknown unknowns. You can count how many new constraints turn up each week.

item.title: Where's the Spool?
item.description: A pipe spool gets fabricated, shipped, received, staged and installed, and each step lives in a different system. Finding one still takes three phone calls and a walk through the laydown yard.

item.title: If Signing Is a Chore, Signatures Mean Nothing
item.description: A hold-point signature can mean a drive across site, a binder and a wet pen. So people batch them up, or sign without looking.

item.title: Should foremen see the whole schedule?
item.description: Probably not. Three weeks of their own work and what is blocking it. The rest is noise until it isn't.

item.title: A PDF Procedure Is a Suggestion
item.description: A procedure in a PDF is advice. What the crew does is a sequence of steps, checks, hold points and qualifications, whatever the document looks like.

item.title: Which Constraint Do We Clear Today?
item.description: Status meetings ask what happened yesterday. The question that matters is which blocked item, cleared today, frees up the most work.

item.title: Does a good-looking Gantt chart mean a good plan?
item.description: No. A messy one that was updated this morning beats a tidy one from last month.

item.title: The Critical Path Moves
item.description: Run a schedule through a thousand simulations of weather and deliveries and the critical path often changes from run to run. The one on the printout is just one of those runs.

item.title: Assumptions Expire
item.description: Ground conditions, vendor capacity, "the permit will renew": written down at sanction and never read again. An assumption is a risk nobody has checked yet.

item.title: Baselines Go Stale
item.description: Two winters and forty change orders after sanction, the job is still measured against the sanction-day plan, and the gap gets called variance.

item.title: The CN Tower: Pouring a Tower Without Stopping
item.description: Built in about three and a half years in the 1970s, the CN Tower rose on a continuously moving concrete form and was topped by a helicopter. Most of its lessons are about method and sequence.

item.title: Why does winter cost more than the heat?
item.description: Parkas, short days, frozen equipment, and Monday mornings spent thawing things out. The fuel bill is the part you can see.

item.title: The Whiteboard and the Schedule Drift Apart
item.description: The schedule has five thousand activities. The site runs off a whiteboard three weeks deep, updated at 6 a.m. Both are needed: the contract needs the full record, and the crew needs this week.

item.title: Everything Is a Constraint
item.description: A predecessor, a missing spool, an unsigned permit, a crane booked elsewhere, wind over the lift limit, a room too crowded to work in, a dose budget nearly spent. Seven systems manage them. They're all the same thing: something that has to be true before work can start.

item.title: Who should run the lessons-learned session?
item.description: Someone who wasn't on the job. People tell an outsider things they won't say to their boss.

item.title: Forty Days of Float, One Day Left
item.description: A pour needs three dry days. The crane leaves in October. In-water work stops when the fish come back. None of those are logic ties, and most schedules don't model them.

item.title: Dave Is at a Wedding
item.description: The schedule says two Class B welders. The job needs Dave, the only one qualified on that alloy, and Dave is at his daughter's wedding until Tuesday.

item.title: How many crane picks fit in an hour?
item.description: Fewer than the plan says. Rigging, signals and wind eat more of the hour than the lift does.

item.title: Stop Retyping the Foreman's Diary
item.description: Foremen write down what happened every day. Then the same facts get retyped into the schedule update, the timesheet, an RFI, a QC record and, years later, a claim.

item.title: Four Breakdowns, Four Projects
item.description: The estimate, schedule, cost report and work packages each have a breakdown structure. They match on sanction day. By month six there are four versions and a standing meeting to reconcile them.

item.title: Green Needs a Signature
item.description: Anyone can mark a status green, so reports drift optimistic. Often green just means nobody wanted the argument.

item.title: What should a new PM do on day one?
item.description: Walk the site with the superintendent and listen. Read the schedule on day two.

item.title: How Sure Are We About the Finish?
item.description: SPI and CPI measure work done against the plan. Nothing measures how well we know the finish date, and that's what the owner is paying for. A job can report green every month while it gets later.
